overview: The Free City of Kraków was a small republic created in 1815 under the protection and supervision of Austria, Prussia and Russia. It included surrounding countryside as well as the city. Austria annexed it in 1846; the atlas’s 1878 endpoint belongs to map coverage, not continuing republican independence.

periods.title: A limited constitutional experiment
periods.summary: The new republic had its own institutions within an international protectorate.

periods.title: Increasing outside pressure
periods.summary: Foreign occupations and tighter supervision narrowed the republic’s room for political action.

sections.title: A small republic with powerful neighbors

items.text: The state included Kraków, seventeen rural communes and three privately owned small towns: Chrzanów, Trzebinia and Nowa Góra. Its story therefore includes villagers and small-town residents, rather than only the people living around Kraków’s famous market square.

A Governing Senate and an Assembly of Representatives handled legislation and administration. University and cathedral representatives also participated in the political structure. The protecting powers could intervene above these institutions, and eventually controlled Senate appointments: the word “free” did not mean unrestricted sovereignty.

Different legal inheritances coexisted, including the Napoleonic Code, Austrian rules and the republic’s own legislation. Officials and residents had to work through this layered legal landscape. A border or government changing did not automatically replace every rule governing property and disputes.

Between 1822 and 1830, former fortifications became much of the public garden now called Planty. A stretch around the Barbican and St Florian’s Gate survived. Space once meant to keep people out became a place where residents could walk around their city.

After 1826, work extended around Wawel Hill, with vineyards and peach orchards on its southern slopes. Later Austrian military rebuilding destroyed them. The republic’s landscape included productive gardens as well as monuments: there were peaches below the royal hill.

Czernichów’s school history records that residents paid contributions toward a new school building in 1839, ordered by the republic’s Senate. This connects a national decision with money raised locally. It was a village classroom project, distinct from the agricultural school founded there much later.

The 1817 regulations reorganized Kraków’s Jewish communal administration. Committees oversaw welfare, charity and the hospital. These arrangements show a community providing care while negotiating a state that increasingly directed its internal institutions.

A Jewish school with a Polish curriculum moved into Kazimierz’s town hall in 1835. Families faced pressures about language, schooling and residence: officials made some privileges conditional on clothing, education and wealth. The republic’s liberal reputation must be read alongside these discriminatory conditions.

At the university, Walenty Litwiński taught criminal law and procedure using European legal scholarship. He was elected rector repeatedly between 1814 and 1821 and also played a political role. The city’s university was part of its civic life as well as a place for lectures.

sections.title: Memorials, a message and the end

items.text: Kościuszko’s commemorative mound was built between 1820 and 1823 by paid local workers and volunteers, including visitors. Soil from places associated with his battles became part of it. Building a memorial was a shared physical undertaking: people helped make the hill, not just admire it.

In 1838 the Senate ordered a medal honoring Florian Straszewski’s work improving the city. Its Polish inscription ends “Senat i lud Krakowa”: “The Senate and people of Kraków.” This short writing sample belongs to a dated commemorative object, linking public gratitude to the new gardens.

A deposit placed in St Mary’s church-tower finial in 1843 included a city plan, newspaper, coins and a Straszewski medal, recorded when the finial was opened in 1912. A church roof could double as an archive deliberately left for future readers.

Foreign troops occupied Kraków in 1831 and again from 1836, when forces of the three protecting powers entered. Austrian troops stayed until 1841. After the failed uprising of 1846, Austria incorporated the city and district into its monarchy, ending the republic’s separate political institutions.

ending.text: Austria annexed the Free City after the uprising of 1846. The republic ended, while Kraków’s residents, university, religious communities and public gardens continued within a different state. The imported outline remaining until 1878 does not preserve its former constitutional status.
